chunk_findings.detail: The old function could index `data["hooks"]["SessionStart"]` directly because the install path always created exactly that key, so absence was unrepresentable. This change makes the key a caller-supplied `event` but keeps direct indexing: `if kept_groups: data["hooks"][event] = kept_groups` / `else: del data["hooks"][event]`, and the loop above the hunk that populates `kept_groups` reads the same parameterized key. For the new `UserPromptSubmit` event the key does not exist in any settings file written before this change (i.e. every existing user's `~/.claude/settings.json`). Running the generalized uninstall against such a file — e.g. `ddflow hooks uninstall --claude` on an unmodified pre-upgrade config, or any caller that uninstalls each supported event rather than only the keys present in the file — reaches `del data["hooks"][event]` (or the `data["hooks"][event]` loop header) with no `UserPromptSubmit` entry and raises `KeyError`. The intended graceful result, `no ddflow UserPromptSubmit hook in <path>`, is unreachable for that case: `if not removed: return ...` only executes after the event's group list has already been iterated successfully, so it only covers "key present, no ddflow hook inside", not "key absent". The failure mode is a traceback and an unmodified/partially-processed settings file rather than the documented no-op. Reaching the same line with the key absent is only avoided if the (unseen) caller filters to existing events or the function guards `event not in data["hooks"]` before the loop; neither guard is present in the reviewed change, and the new parameterization is what makes the absent-key case reachable in the first place.

chunk_findings.detail: `_recorded_recently` never receives or checks the session the event belongs to: it matches on `ev.data["text"] == clean` plus the age window alone, even though the stated intent is "same session + text within a short window". Because `capture_prompt` keys the auto record on `h-<harness_id>` while `prompt` is called with the agent's own ddflow session id, the two writers are *different* sessions, so the only thing that ever makes them line up is the fact that session is ignored — and that same omission makes unrelated sessions collide. Concrete failure: two Claude Code sessions run in parallel (different `session_id`s → different `h-…` subjects). Session A's UserPromptSubmit records auto `"continue"` at T. One second later session B's hook fires for its own genuine `"continue"`; `capture_prompt` for B scans, finds A's auto event with age < `DOUBLE_FIRE_S` (3s), returns `"duplicate"` and never appends B's prompt. When B's agent then calls `session_prompt`, `prompt()` scans with `auto_only=True`/`window=120`, again finds A's auto record, returns `n` and appends nothing either. B's prompt is now lost everywhere — the exact thing this change exists to prevent. The same over-match drops legitimate agent prompts from any agent without a prompt hook (a "known gap" harness) whose text matches some other session's auto capture within 120s, and short prompts (`"y"`, `"yes"`, `"continue"`, `"go"`) are the most likely to collide.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py `_recorded_recently` / `capture_prompt` / `prompt`

chunk_findings.detail: `re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9._-]", "", str(raw))[:64]` can map distinct harness session ids onto the same ddflow session. Any two ids that differ only in stripped characters (e.g. `"conv/abc"` vs `"convabc"`, or ids from a harness that uses `:`/`/` separators) both become `h-convabc`, and any two ids sharing a 64-char prefix are truncated to the same value. Since `capture_prompt` reuses a session whenever `session.started` with that subject exists, prompts and `session.started` from two different conversations are silently merged into one session, and the text-only dedupe above then cross-suppresses between them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py `harness_session_id`

chunk_findings.detail: `_hook_stdin` multiplexes stdin through `select.select([fd], [], [], left)`, but on Windows Python's `select` is implemented over Winsock and only accepts socket handles. The actual hook invocation supplies stdin as a *pipe* (or other CRT file descriptor), so `select.select` raises `OSError: [WinError 10038]` on the very first call. Because the whole body is wrapped in `except Exception: return ""`, this is swallowed: `_hook_stdin` returns an empty string, `A.hooks` receives `stdin=""`, and the UserPromptSubmit / BeforeAgent hook silently records nothing — on every prompt, with no error or diagnostic. The feature is a total no-op in that environment, which directly contradicts the stated goal of "record every operator prompt automatically." A platform-independent read (e.g. `threading`/`subprocess`-based read, or `os.read` guarded by `selectors`/`msvcrt` on Windows, or simply reading the already-buffered stdin when `select` is unavailable) is needed; at minimum the bare `except` hides the failure instead of falling back.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/setup.py:253 (`_hook_stdin`)

chunk_findings.detail: The first `_hook` records the prompt under the harness session `s1`, whose event subject is `h-s1` (as `test_hook_json_records_one_prompt_in_a_session_keyed_on_the_harness_id` explicitly asserts), while the agent call records under `s-agent`. Requiring `len(_events(repo, "session.prompt")) == 1` therefore forces dedupe on text ignoring the session, contradicting the stated intent to dedupe only "same session + text within a short window". A correct same-session implementation would produce two events here and fail this assertion; conversely the implementation this test mandates silently drops a legitimate second prompt whenever two different sessions send the same text (e.g. both operators type "yes" within the dedupe window), defeating the change's goal of recording every operator prompt.

chunk_findings.detail: The test discards the hook's captured stderr (line 76) and scans only files under `.ddflow` (line 77). An implementation that prints the raw prompt to stderr before redaction, or that emits it on stdout, passes this test even though the secret has escaped the process into the harness's hook logs/transcript. The assertion should also verify `SECRET not in err` and `SECRET not in out`.

chunk_findings.detail: On Windows the fallback reads via `sys.stdin.read()` (text mode, locale codec) instead of reading bytes and decoding UTF-8 like the primary path. Given a hook payload with a non-ASCII prompt, the recorded `session.prompt` text is mojibake (e.g. `"café"` -> `"cafÃ©"`), and for prompts containing bytes undefined in the ANSI code page the `UnicodeDecodeError` is swallowed by the inner `except Exception: pass`, `box` stays empty, and the prompt is dropped entirely. The fallback should read the same byte stream (`os.read(fd, ...)` / `sys.stdin.buffer.read()`) and decode with the same `utf-8`/`replace` policy so the Windows path records the same text as the POSIX path.

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback runs whenever the `select` path raises, which on Windows is the *normal* path (`select.select` only accepts sockets there, so a pipe fd raises `OSError`). It does `sys.stdin.buffer.read()`, which blocks until **EOF**, not until data is available, and then abandons the thread with `t.join(timeout_s)` and returns `""`. So if the harness writes the complete hook JSON but does not close the pipe within `timeout_s` (a long-lived stdin pipe), the bytes are discarded and the prompt is never recorded. The POSIX path does not have this behaviour: its loop appends whatever `os.read` returned and, when the deadline passes, returns `b"".join(chunks)`, i.e. the JSON that already arrived. Concretely: on Windows, a harness that writes `{"session_id":"s1","prompt":"deploy"}\n` and leaves stdin open records nothing, while the identical input on Linux/macOS records the prompt. The "never block the turn" goal is preserved, but "record every operator prompt" is not, and the fallback returns an empty string that is indistinguishable from a genuinely silent pipe.

chunk_findings.detail:
The comment claims "a digest keeps them apart," but the mapping is still not injective, and the digest is skipped exactly in the cases that need it. Two counterexamples:
- Any two ids that sanitise to empty collide: `harness_session_id("///")` and `harness_session_id("***")` both hit `if not safe: return ""` and produce `""`.
- Even in the digest branch, `raw2 = raw1_sanitised + "-" + sha256(raw1)[:16]` collides with `raw1`: e.g. `raw1 = "a!"` yields `"h-a-" + sha256("a!")[:16]`, and `raw2 = "a-" + sha256("a!")[:16]` is itself all-valid so `safe == raw2` and it returns the identical id.
When two distinct harness ids map to one ddflow id, they share one `session.started`/subject: `capture_prompt`'s new `subject=sid` filter (and, for the empty case, the falsy `subject` guard that disables the filter entirely) then treats two different conversations as one and can drop the second conversation's identical-text prompt as a "duplicate".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py `harness_session_id`

chunk_findings.detail: The test's own comment states that "the PR-merge settle path calls CM.verdict directly, not api.complete", and the function name claims the check is carried by the verdict so *every* completion path enforces it. But the body never exercises that path: it constructs a bare `State`, monkey-places a duck-typed `type("I", (), {"kind": "phase", "state": "done"})()` into `st.items`, and asserts only on the standalone helper `phase_overdue(st, cfg)`. A change that makes `CM.verdict` build its unmet conditions from a different source, or that forgets to fold the phase-overdue result into the verdict (while leaving `phase_overdue` intact), leaves this test green and the settle/PR-merge completion path silently able to complete a phase with an overdue architecture review — the exact gap the test is named after. To actually cover the claim the test would have to invoke `CM.verdict` (or the settle path) on a state with an overdue phase pass and assert on the returned conditions/refusal, rather than importing and calling the helper the verdict is supposed to call.
